the molecular basis of protein–protein and protein–DNA interactions of a type II toxin–antitoxins system, which has been found in many bacterial genomes.

the molecular basis of HicA–induced destabilization of the HicB:DNA interaction, which has implications in the regulation of TA systems and bacterial physiology and pathogenicity.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HicA is a toxin that destabilizes a DNA–antitoxins complex by a cooperative binding mechanism.
the HicA toxin destabilizes the HICB–DNA complex through a cooperative process.

The main takeaway from our work is that
HicB is a tetramer that forms an octameric complex with HicA.
HicA and other TA toxins can act by destabilizing TA antitoxin–DNA complexes, rather than by direct binding to DNA.
HicA is a potent DNA binding inhibitor of HicB, and that this is a general feature of TA toxins that bind DNA, and not just the HicA toxin.
